sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Utilitarian Influence**: Guided by the philosophies of Jeremy Bentham and James Mill, aiming for 'the greatest happiness of the greatest number' through rationalized administration.
• **Financial Retrenchment**: Inherited a depleted treasury due to the First Anglo-Burmese War; implemented strict economic measures in civil and military expenditures to achieve a surplus.
• **Liberal Humanitarianism**: Marked a departure from non-intervention to active legislative interference in deep-rooted social evils like **Sati** and **Thuggee**.
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Centralization of legislative authority via the **Charter Act of 1833**, making the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India.

items.definition: The landmark legislation passed by William Bentinck declaring the practice of Sati illegal and punishable in criminal courts as culpable homicide.
The official minute that tipped the scale in favor of English as the medium of instruction in higher education over Oriental languages.
Ended the commercial activities of the East India Company, made it purely an administrative body, and centralized legislative powers in the Governor-General-in-Council.
Specialized branch led by Major William Sleeman using systemic intelligence-gathering and approvers to eradicate hereditary highway robbery and ritual murder.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Bengal Presidency**: Center of administrative centralization and the primary hub for the implementation of English education and judicial restructuring.
• **Central and Upper India (Doab, Bundelkhand)**: Primary zones for the operations against the Thugs, alongside pacification and revenue settlements under the Mahalwari system.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Resistance from orthodox native society regarding social legislation; administrative dislocation caused by abolishing provincial courts.
• **Policy Interventions**: Careful consultation with local elites, employment of Indian judicial personnel (Sadaj Amin/Munsiffs), and systematic revenue assessments.

items.title: Mnemonic for Bentinck's Major Reforms
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: 'S-E-T-C' (Sati, Education, Thuggee, Charter).
• **Decoded Meaning**: Sati abolished (1829), English Education introduced (1835), Thuggee suppressed (1830s), Charter Act passed (1833).
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly chronologically aligns Bentinck's major contributions without confusion with Dalhousie or Curzon.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Bentinck = Benevolent/Budget plus Centralization (1833 Charter + 1829 Sati + 1835 English).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently attributes the introduction of the civil services or police code directly to Bentinck, whereas Cornwallis is the father of the Civil Services and Police, while Bentinck reformed the judiciary by abolishing provincial courts and employing Indians.

Mains Value Addition: Analyze Bentinck's era as the bridging phase where British policy shifted from conservative preservation of traditional institutions to reforming Indian society through western legal and educational paradigms.

keyTakeaways: William Bentinck's tenure (1828–1835) was defined by financial integrity, administrative rationalization, and humanitarian social reforms.
Key legislative landmarks include the abolition of Sati (1829), suppression of Thuggee, the English Education Act (1835), and the Charter Act of 1833.
His judicial reforms dismantled Cornwallis's slow-moving provincial courts and increased Indian participation at lower judicial levels.
